analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to give full cash refunds for canceled or significantly delayed flights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large airlines and ticket sellers to offer travelers a full cash refund — including bag and seat fees — within 30 days if the airline cancels or significantly delays a flight, or if the traveler cancels at least 48 hours ahead. Airlines could still offer vouchers, but any voucher would have to be valid forever and come with a clear notice that cash is available. It would also have let travelers who took vouchers during the COVID-19 travel collapse swap unused voucher value for cash.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers. Anyone whose flight is canceled or badly delayed could get money back instead of being pushed toward a voucher. People who accepted vouchers during the 2020-2021 wave of cancellations could convert unused ones to cash. The upfront disclosure requirement would tell buyers, before they pay, that they can cancel for a full refund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers, including past voucher holders

how_it_helps.text: Requires large airlines and ticket agents to offer a full cash refund, including ancillary fees, within 30 days of a request when the carrier cancels or significantly delays a flight, or the passenger cancels at least 48 hours before departure.
Allows vouchers only if they are valid indefinitely and accompanied by clear notice of the passenger's right to cash, so travelers cannot be steered into expiring credits.
Lets passengers who received vouchers for flights canceled between March 1, 2020 and enactment convert unused voucher value into a cash refund within 30 days of asking.
Requires airlines and ticket agents to tell buyers, before purchase, that they can cancel for a full cash refund.
Attaches a $1,000 civil penalty per violation to give the requirement enforcement teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Major airlines — the bill covers carriers with 2018 operating revenue over $1.5 billion — and ticket agents, who would absorb refund payouts and compliance costs. The bill explicitly allows airlines to use COVID-19 airline relief appropriations (other than CARES Act payroll-support funds) to pay the refunds.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves 'significantly delayed' to be defined later by the Secretary of Transportation, so the exact scope of the refund right — and the costs and litigation around it — would depend on future regulation.
Airlines would bear direct refund costs and compliance costs, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that at least some of that could surface in fares or fees over time.
A passenger could claim a cash refund for only one flight per city-pair itinerary per date, so travelers who booked multi-flight trips and canceled get less protection than the headline suggests.

Requiring cash refunds even for voluntary passenger cancellations 48 hours out would end the nonrefundable-ticket pricing model that lets airlines sell cheaper fares, so some travelers who accept restrictions for lower prices could see fewer of those options.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to travelers is direct and concrete: money back instead of vouchers when a trip falls through, plus a lasting right to convert old COVID-era vouchers to cash. The costs fall on large airlines, which received substantial federal relief during the pandemic and are explicitly allowed to use some of those appropriations to pay refunds. The main design weaknesses are the undefined delay threshold and the one-flight-per-itinerary limit, which narrow the guarantee, but they do not change the bill's basic direction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on February 28, 2023, joined by eight cosponsors — seven Senate Democrats and one Independent.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action appears in the record — no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major airlines and ticket agents, who keep their existing refund and voucher practices rather than facing a statutory cash-refund mandate. Travelers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it as its sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the measure never advanced past committee referral.

against.name: U.S. airline industry
against.role: Major passenger carriers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed mandates requiring cash refunds for canceled and delayed flights during this period, arguing refunds should stay a matter of Department of Transportation rules and that cash mandates would raise costs.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: Carriers with 2018 revenue over $1.5 billion would have had to pay cash refunds within 30 days for canceled or significantly delayed flights and for passenger cancellations 48 hours out, including fees, and could no longer rely on expiring vouchers as the default remedy. That cash liability is the airline industry's interest running against the traveler's, and the industry's public position was that refund rules should remain with regulators rather than statute.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and ticket agents
industries.note: Ticket agents would have to process refunds and make the disclosures, though the bill entitles them to prompt reimbursement from carriers for the fare portion. The compliance burden is real, but the consumer-facing cost is limited.
The bill's retroactive provision would let passengers who accepted vouchers for flights canceled since March 1, 2020 convert unused value into cash.
